title: 5. Effects of vitamin B complex supplementation level on plasma biotin and stress responses in preconditioned beef calves.
content:
Abstract
A study was conducted at the Eastern Oregon Agricultural Research Center (EOARC; Burns, Oregon) to evaluate the effects of supplementation levels of a blend of vitamin B complex offered to weaned beef calves in a 42-day preconditioning program. Sixty-three Angus × Hereford calves were stratified by body weight (BW; 250 ± 4 kg) after weaning (d0) and allocated into 21 pens (3 calves/pen). Pens were randomly assigned to one of three treatments: (1) Control, (2) VitB1g, or (3) VitB2g. Calves assigned to vitamin B supplementation received vitamin B complex (1 vs. 2g/calf daily; Vivalto®, Selko® USA) mixed with 1.3 kg of dried distillers’ grains (DDG), while calves in the Control group received only DDG. All calves had free access to chopped alfalfa-grass hay (14% CP and 59 % TDN) and whole corn. Blood samples were collected on days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 42 to evaluate plasma cortisol and acute phase proteins. Vitamin B7 concentration was measured on days 0, 14 and 42. Variables were analyzed as repeated measures using the MIXED procedure in SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with statistical significance set as P ≤ 0.05. Effects of treatment, day, and the interaction (P ≤ 0.005) were observed for plasma vitamin B7 concentrations. At weaning, all calves had similar (P ≥ 0.91) plasma vitamin B7 concentrations (2.50 ± 0.11 ng/mL). With two weeks of supplementation, on d14, calves assigned to VitB2g treatment had greater (P ≤ 0.005) vitamin B7 concentration (4.70 ± 0.19 ng/mL) than calves assigned to VitB1g and Control treatments which had similar vitamin B7 concentrations (P = 0.79; 3.63 and 3.55 ± 0.19 ng/mL, respectively for VitB1g and Control). At the end of the preconditioning phase, on d42, calves assigned to VitB2g had greater (P ≤ 0.02) vitamin B7 concentrations (4.47 ± 0.19 ng/mL) than calves assigned to VitB1g (3.79 ± 0.19 ng/mL) and Control (3.41 ± 0.19 ng/mL) treatments which continued to remain similar (P = 0.17). Of the stress markers evaluated, a tendency for a treatment × day interaction (P = 0.08) for Cortisol concentration was observed. Cortisol concentrations were similar at weaning (P ≥ 0.89; 2.02 ± 0.9 ug/mL). Interestingly, at the end of the supplementation period, calves supplemented with vitamin B complex, regardless of vitamin level supplementation, had lower cortisol concentration (P ≤ 0.05; 1.90 ± 0.17 ug/mL) than calves assigned to Control treatment (2.46 ± 0.17 ug/mL). Collectively, these findings suggest that vitamin B complex supplementation during preconditioning enhances circulating vitamin B7 concentration, especially at 2 g/d, and may attenuate physiological stress responses in weaned beef calves.
